messages.author: bacb0402e67daa77
messages.subject: Some further questions about code for a multivariate ODE fit w/ missing data
parts:
Hi Stan Developers,

Thank you again for your very patient help in the last thread. I learned a lot from it and profusely apologize for the amount of time I've taken from you guys. A few more issues have been cropping up as I've been coding. I will break them up into parts.

1) I tried returning a real[N,2] derived from my ODE solutions and found that to be impossible, so right now I am jamming my solutions into a real[2*N] and then converting to a vector[N,2] in another block. Would it be possible to return a multi-dimensional array from a function and avoid the "Mismatched array dimensions. Returned expression does not match return type LHS type = real[]; RHS type = real[,]" error?

2) On a related note, is there a vectorized way of doing the operation

for (n in 1:N_t) {
  ratios_hat_vector[n,1] = ratios_hat[n];
  ratios_hat_vector[n,2] = ratios_hat[N_t+n];
}

with a single function? I tried doing the to_vector operation and got the error message, "dimension mismatch in assignment; variable name = ratios_hat_vector, num dimensions given = 1; right-hand side dimensions = 0."

3) I left missing data elements blank on my CSV file, and R fills the those elements with "NA." I thought I could leave that alone, but Stan does not seem to like that and gives me the error message "Error in FUN(X[[i]], ...) : Stan does not support NA (in CO2_flux_ratios) in data failed to preprocess the data; sampling not done." What should I fill in then for missing data elements in my CSV file? I thought I could simply ignore the NA's previously.

4) Per our last discussion, I took Bob and Michael's advice and "ignore" rather than impute the missing data such that sometimes likelihood incorporates both measurements, and other times only uses the one available measurement. In my code which I've attached, I have the following lines based on Bob's example code in the previous thread:

//likelihood
ratios_vector[obs12] ~ multi_normal(ratios_hat_vector[obs12], Sigma); // Fit elements with both entries
ratios_vector[obs1,1] ~ normal(ratios_hat_vector[obs1,1], Sigma[1,1]); // Fit elements with only flux ratio entries
ratios_vector[obs2,2] ~ normal(ratios_hat_vector[obs2,2], Sigma[2,2]); // Fit elements with only microbial ratio entries

(I am not sure I can use this notation, since obs12, obs1, obs2 are arrays of ints that list the indices for which ratios_vector has both elements, is missing one element, and is missing the other element, respectively. I just have it in there for now in the hopes that this will work for vectorization.) Sigma[1,1] and Sigma[2,2] represent measurement error/misprediction for each measurement. Can I assume the covariance as 0 for the Sigma matrix just to have slightly fewer varying parameters?


---------

Again, many thanks for all your help. As someone who came from a biology background and fell into a computational PhD topic, I've been struggling a lot with the pedagogy of the stats courses at my institution, and would be utterly lost without help from this Google Group. I've been relying heavily on reading Bob's code examples and rewatching Michael's videos on Youtube. I would gladly order a pizza for all of you guys in appreciation if you weren't geographically spread out.

parts:
> On Nov 27, 2016, at 3:00 AM, H. X. <yaois...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Stan Developers,
>
> Thank you again for your very patient help in the last thread. I learned a lot from it and profusely apologize for the amount of time I've taken from you guys. A few more issues have been cropping up as I've been coding. I will break them up into parts.
>
> 1) I tried returning a real[N,2] derived from my ODE solutions and found that to be impossible, so right now I am jamming my solutions into a real[2*N] and then converting to a vector[N,2] in another block. Would it be possible to return a multi-dimensional array from a function and avoid the "Mismatched array dimensions. Returned expression does not match return type LHS type = real[]; RHS type = real[,]" error?

I'm not quite sure what you're asking. The ODE solver returns a 2D
array (that is, a real[,] type). Your solutions come out in a time x state
array.

> 2) On a related note, is there a vectorized way of doing the operation
>
> for (n in 1:N_t) {
> ratios_hat_vector[n,1] = ratios_hat[n];
> ratios_hat_vector[n,2] = ratios_hat[N_t+n];
> }
>
> with a single function? I tried doing the to_vector operation and got the error message, "dimension mismatch in assignment; variable name = ratios_hat_vector, num dimensions given = 1; right-hand side dimensions = 0."

ratios_hat_vector[ , 1] = ratios_hat[1:N_t];
ratios_hat_vector[ , 2] = ratios_hat[(N_t + 1):(2 * N_t)];

>
> 3) I left missing data elements blank on my CSV file, and R fills the those elements with "NA." I thought I could leave that alone, but Stan does not seem to like that and gives me the error message "Error in FUN(X[[i]], ...) : Stan does not support NA (in CO2_flux_ratios) in data failed to preprocess the data; sampling not done." What should I fill in then for missing data elements in my CSV file? I thought I could simply ignore the NA's previously.

No. See the manual chapter on missing data. Stan doesn't
accept NA values in any form under any coding. You either
need to use a sparse encoding of the variables that are there
(see the ragged and sparse structure) or you need to do as
I suggested last time and pass in dummy values and then a separate
indexing of where values show up.

> 4) Per our last discussion, I took Bob and Michael's advice and "ignore" rather than impute the missing data such that sometimes likelihood incorporates both measurements, and other times only uses the one available measurement. In my code which I've attached, I have the following lines based on Bob's example code in the previous thread:
>
> //likelihood
> ratios_vector[obs12] ~ multi_normal(ratios_hat_vector[obs12], Sigma); // Fit elements with both entries
> ratios_vector[obs1,1] ~ normal(ratios_hat_vector[obs1,1], Sigma[1,1]); // Fit elements with only flux ratio entries
> ratios_vector[obs2,2] ~ normal(ratios_hat_vector[obs2,2], Sigma[2,2]); // Fit elements with only microbial ratio entries
>
> (I am not sure I can use this notation, since obs12, obs1, obs2 are arrays of ints that list the indices for which ratios_vector has both elements, is missing one element, and is missing the other element, respectively. I just have it in there for now in the hopes that this will work for vectorization.)

Try working up from simple examples to see that
things work the way you expect.

But I think the answer is that yes, what you have here
will work. But if those observations really are observations,
you're better off storing away the results in transformed
data so you only have to compute it once.
> Sigma[1,1] and Sigma[2,2] represent measurement error/misprediction for each measurement. Can I assume the covariance as 0 for the Sigma matrix just to have slightly fewer varying parameters?

Sure, then you don't need multi_normal and everything gets
much easier.

- Bob

easily do with a (multivariate) normal.

parts: Functions can output whatever you declare them to output.

> On Nov 28, 2016, at 2:25 PM, H. X. <yaois...@gmail.com> wrote:

However, I have to further transform my solutions because my data comes in the form of ratios, and I have another function which converts the solutions to ratios. Functions only seem to be able to output real[]'s, rather than real[,]s.

Functions can return whatever you declare them to output.
But the system ODE function has a fixed signature that has
to conform exactly.

> But I think the answer is that yes, what you have here
> will work. But if those observations really are observations,
> you're better off storing away the results in transformed
> data so you only have to compute it once.
>
> I'm not entirely clear on this, I apologize. So my ratios_vector is in my transformed data block. I also compute obs12, obs1, and obs2, which are the indices denoting corresponding columns of the bivariate vector that have both elements or are missing one, in the transformed data block. This is what you mean, right?
Yes.

> Sure, then you don't need multi_normal and everything gets
> much easier.
>
> So I can feed my bivariate vector into normal, such that I have data ~ normal(model,Sigma)? Or do I separate my bivariate vector into two vectors and feed each into normal such that I have data[,1] ~ normal(model,sigma1), data[,2] ~ normal(model,sigma2)?

I was just assuming you had a multivariate distribution like a multinormal,
and that some of the dimensions might be missing. My illustration was for
how to code the marginalizations efficiently in two dimensions. So yes,
those just get fed into the normal when one's missing because that's the marginal
distribution of one parameter.

- Bob

is acting like the linear predictor in a multivariate regression
and hence defines mu (sometimes people like to call that y_hat,
but I don't like to mix estimation notation into my clean Bayesian
models).

- Bob
